To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

working memory spans in the Sternberg task vary as a function not only of the time allowed to respond, as predicted by the standard time-based model (e.g., Cowan, 1988), but also of the cognitive load of intervening tasks.
working memory spans are determined by the time constraints of the processing task and that the maintenance component is affected by both the number of retrievals and the time allowed for them.

working memory span is a function of the cognitive load of processing and that the latter is determined by the number of memory traces that need to be retrieved and the time allowed for the processing of those traces.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of whether the cognitive load of a working memory task affects working memory performance.
the nature of working memory and the factors that influence its performance.
the question of how working memory spans vary with the cognitive load of processing.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the time-based resource sharing model accounts well for the results of the experiments presented in this article, and the model provides a good account of the results of the other studies that have been published so far on working memory span in adults.
the time-based resource sharing model provides a new theoretical framework for the study of working memory that accounts for the effects of time and resource sharing in a single model.
, in the context of working memory spans, resource sharing is a more appropriate metaphor than resource competition.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the capacity of working memory in adults is limited by time constraints.

we have shown that the capacity of working memory is determined by the number of items to be remembered, the time allowed to remember them, and the number of items that must be processed during that time.
the time-based resource sharing model is an important step forward in understanding the cognitive processes that underlie working memory spans.
The main takeaway from our work is that

working memory spans are not limited by the number of items to be maintained in memory but by the cognitive load of a task that is performed concurrently with the maintenance of the to-be-recalled items.

the cognitive load of working memory tasks depends on the number of items to be maintained, the time allowed to process the items, and the number of intervening memory retrievals required to perform the task.
working memory spans are determined by a trade-off between the cognitive load of a processing task and the time allowed for it.
